extracted.intended_audience: literate early-18th-century London reading public (readers of The Spectator); general readers interested in morals, manners, and literary criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted rubrics concern moral conduct, social manners, and principles of literary criticism as presented in Spectator essays (short moral/literary periodical pieces).

rubrics_metrics.name: Generosity should be founded in frugality
rubrics_metrics.description: “all Liberality should have for its Basis and Support Frugality.” (Steele) — liberality ought to flow from reasoned prudence rather than loose and unguarded temper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generosity is laudable only when it does not exhaust a man's capacity to continue doing good; it should be a rational, sustainable practice rather than an impulsive sacrifice that destroys future ability to assist. Anti-patterns: generosity that reduces a man's fortune below the capacity to act according to his natural temper; giving from passion rather than conviction. Examples/notes from the essay: a generous man who sacrifices opportunities to help later is foolish; the maxim is used to criticise ostentatious public largesses and to recommend measured, long-term beneficence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benignity in commerce (fair trader conduct)
rubrics_metrics.description: “A constant Benignity in Commerce with the rest of the World, which ought to run through all a Man's Actions,” i.e., a trader should be frank in kindnesses, abhor severity in demands, be just and easy in buying, selling, lending, and neighbourly acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commercial life affords opportunities to practise the highest fruit of wealth (being liberal without expending personal fortune) by fair dealing and support of industrious people. Recommended behaviours: be just and easy in transactions, avoid needless disputes, protect industrious men from bankruptcy, and labour to improve the fortunes of those you deal with. Anti-patterns: harshness, pride, or vengeful extraction of payment from those already ruined; ostentatious charity that breeds envy rather than public good. Example: the practising citizen who quietly aids others versus public entertainments/largesses that are vicious or ill-timed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceal favors to avoid invidiousness
rubrics_metrics.description: “He who obliges is as much concerned to keep the Favour a Secret, as he who receives it.” — discretion in bestowing favours prevents envy and political/social attack.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publicizing beneficence often provokes envy or political retaliation; concealment shields both the benefactor and the beneficiary and avoids making virtuous acts invidious. Example: Tom the Bounteous conceals his compassion under a rough outward manner, and the author confesses having to understate good deeds when political partisanship would make praise dangerous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Civic duty to support public funds
rubrics_metrics.description: A man who does not 'imbark some part of his Fortune with the State' cannot be called a good subject — contributing to public funds is a form of benignity and public obligation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investing part of one's fortune in public/State funds is recommended as a way to extend one's beneficence broadly and to discharge civic obligations. This practice both supports state security and spreads obligations/benefits more widely than private largesses alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid detraction and suppression of merit in society
rubrics_metrics.description: The essayist condemns 'all manner of Detraction' and the habit of diminishing those who are commended; maligning the praised or whispering calumnies suppresses merit and discourages worthy behaviour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Social conversation that systematically undercuts praise (by inventing faults or recounting pedigrees/methods of acquisition) is vicious: it prevents deserving people from exerting their gifts for public good and dissuades young talent from public engagement. Anti-patterns: the conversational practice exemplified by 'Jack Triplett' who records and repeats malicious exceptions to anyone praised. Suggested response: public animadversion on the habit of detraction to encourage civility and the flourishing of merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reserve ultimate praise until a life is complete; value constancy of character
rubrics_metrics.description: “We are naturally averse to the launching out into a Man's Praise till his Head is laid in the Dust.” — a life may change; death closes reputation and determines it as good or bad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because a person's character and conduct may alter during life, full and definitive praise is safest after death when the course of life is complete. Excellence is especially admirable when a person preserves uniformity of action through life to death; constancy at the end of life confirms character. Examples: Epaminondas's remark ‘You must first see us die,’ contrasting Petronius (cheerful but loose life) and Socrates or Sir Thomas More (consistency between life and death). Anti-patterns: premature, unqualified laudation that fails to account for later changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: True courage must be guided by justice, humanity, and modesty
rubrics_metrics.description: “Courage, without regard to Justice and Humanity, was no other than the Fierceness of a wild Beast.” True magnanimity combines bravery with reason, honour, and concern for others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bravery is praiseworthy only when accompanied by moral sensibility and the capacity for generosity; mere boldness or ostentation is vanity or brutality. True courage shows as quiet, steady resolve and modest deportment rather than noisy, overbearing bravado. Examples: the Ipswich corn-ship master's defence and the privateer's cruel revenge; anti-patterns include youths who are noisy and shameless or those whose ostentatious courage lacks humaneness or justice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propriety in expression; prefer the 'just and sublime' to turgid bombast
rubrics_metrics.description: “There is a Propriety in all things; ... what you Scholars call just and sublime, in opposition to turgid and bombast Expression.” — good writing/speech uses judgment and restraint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers and speakers should avoid improper warmth or inflated, bombastic language; measured expression and modesty manifest true force of genius. Applied to manners, modest behaviour signals greatness of spirit; applied to criticism and composition, clarity and appropriateness trump ostentatious phrase-making. Anti-pattern: rhetorical turgidity that seeks effect without propriety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epic poets may embellish sparse historical material but should preserve principal traditional particulars
rubrics_metrics.description: Virgil 'took the matters of Fact as they came down to him, and circumstanced them after his own manner' — when history or tradition supplies few particulars, the poet may invent, but should weave in the main traditional elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A poet adapting an old or thinly-attested story can and should use invention to fill gaps, but must keep key traditional facts and the character traits associated with them (e.g., Æneas's piety and observance of prodigies). Embellishment should make the story natural, agreeable, or surprising without contradicting established tradition. Example: Virgil retains Roman-believed particulars about Æneas and reworks them artistically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle incredible or ludicrous incidents by qualifying them or placing them appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: When a poet must include astonishing or seemingly ridiculous matter, qualify it (e.g., say it is justified by tradition) and place ludicrous lines in mouths or situations where they are plausible (e.g., a boy's remark).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To prevent absurdity, the writer should (a) explicitly acknowledge that an incident is extraordinary but attested by tradition (Virgil’s preface to the transformation of the fleet), and/or (b) present a ludicrous utterance through a character for whom it will seem natural (e.g., Ascanius's 'We are eating our tables' turns a grotesque prophecy into a charming boyish witticism). Anti-patterns: presenting ludicrous events bluntly or with mismatched tone/voice so they become ridiculous rather than effective.
